multiplication.text: Multiplication means adding equal groups. When we say three times four, we mean three groups with four in each group.
Look at the rows. Count them all: four, eight, twelve. Three rows of four make twelve. So three times four equals twelve.
Here is a trick. Three times four and four times three give the same answer. You can flip the numbers to make it easier.
For the harder facts, skip count. For seven times three, count by sevens: seven, fourteen, twenty-one.

division.text: Division is sharing fairly. Twelve cookies shared with three friends. How many does each friend get?
Let's deal them out fairly: one for you, one for you, one for you, and again, until they are all gone. Each of the three friends gets four cookies. So twelve divided by three equals four.
Division is the opposite of multiplication. Because three times four is twelve, twelve divided by three is four. Use your times tables backwards!

fractions.text: A fraction shows part of a whole. The bottom number tells how many equal pieces the whole is cut into, and the top number tells how many of those pieces we have.
Watch this. Two fourths covers the same amount of space as one half. They look like different numbers, but they are the exact same amount. We call those equivalent fractions.
When the bottom numbers match, the fraction with more pieces on top is the bigger one. Three fifths is more than two fifths because three pieces is more than two pieces.

When the top numbers are the same, look at the size of the pieces. The fewer pieces a whole is cut into, the bigger each piece is. So one half is more than one third. This trick only works when the tops match!

When the tops and the bottoms are both different, the fewer pieces trick can fool you. Make the bottoms match first. Two fifths is the same as four tenths, and four tenths is less than seven tenths. So seven tenths is bigger.

placeValue.text: Every digit sits in a special place. From the right, we have ones, then tens, then hundreds, then thousands. The place a digit sits in tells you its value.
Here is the secret of place value. Ten ones bundle together to make one ten. Ten tens bundle together to make one hundred. So each place is worth ten times the place to its right.
Look at the number one thousand two hundred thirty-four. The two is sitting in the hundreds place, so it is not just two. It really means two hundred.
To round to the nearest ten, look at the ones digit. If it is five or more, round up to the next ten. If it is less than five, round down and keep the ten you already have.

measurement.text: Area is the amount of space inside a shape. You can count all the little squares that fit inside, or take a shortcut and multiply the length times the width. Four times three equals twelve!
Perimeter is the distance all the way around a shape, like walking around the edge of a yard. Add up every side: four plus three plus four plus three equals fourteen.
On a clock, the short hand points to the hour. The long hand points to the minutes, and it counts by fives: five, ten, fifteen. The short hand is just past the eight, so it is eight fifteen!
When you count money, count the dollars first: one dollar. Then count the cents: twenty-five, fifty, seventy-five. Put them together, and you have one dollar and seventy-five cents!

geometry.text: Shapes get their names from their sides and their corners. A square is special because it has four sides that are all the same length, and it has four corners.
Count the sides to name a shape. Three sides make a triangle. Four sides make a quadrilateral. Five sides make a pentagon, and six sides make a hexagon!
A corner, where two sides meet, is called an angle. The square corner that you see in a square is a special angle that we call a right angle.
An angle smaller than a right angle is called acute. It is narrow, like the tip of a pizza slice. An angle bigger than a right angle is called obtuse. It opens up wide.
Lines that run side by side and never cross are called parallel, like train tracks. Lines that cross to make square corners are called perpendicular, like a plus sign.
Let us check what you remember about a square. Think about its straight edges and count them carefully.

dataGraph.text: To collect data, make one tally mark for each fruit sold. The fifth mark crosses the other four, making a bundle of five. Count the bundle as five, then six, seven, eight. Eight plums!
A bar graph shows amounts using bars. Each bar stands for one thing, and the taller a bar is, the bigger its number. A short bar means a small number.
To read a bar, find its top, then slide straight across to the numbers on the side. The apple bar lines up with five, so five apples were sold. The tallest bar shows the biggest number.
How many more plums were sold than apples? Draw a line across from the top of the apple bar. The plum bar reaches three spaces higher: six, seven, eight. Eight minus five equals three!

wordProblem.text: First, read the problem slowly: A box has six rows of four crayons. How many crayons are there in all? Then picture the story in your mind. See the box, and the crayons lined up inside it.
Next, find the question the problem is asking, and then choose the right operation. When the story has equal groups, like rows that are all the same size, that is a clue to multiply.

Now solve it. There are six rows, and each row has four crayons, so we multiply six times four. Count by fours: four, eight, twelve, sixteen, twenty, twenty-four! There are twenty-four crayons in all.

reading.text: Good readers look for the main idea: what the whole passage is mostly about. Read each sentence and ask, who or what is it about? Frogs. Frogs. Frogs! So this passage is mostly about frogs.
Think of the main idea as a tabletop. The details are the legs that hold it up. Frogs live near ponds. Frogs eat insects. Frogs can jump far. Each detail tells us more about frogs.
For a detail question, go back into the text and find the exact words. Don’t guess from memory! What do frogs eat? Find the clue word, eat, in the passage. There it is: they eat insects.

Sometimes the answer is not written down, so you use clues. The text says frogs can jump very far. What do you know about jumping far? It takes strong legs! Clues plus what you know make an inference.

writing.text: A complete sentence has two parts. The naming part tells who or what the sentence is about. The action part tells what they do. And every sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a punctuation mark.
Here is an example. The dog ran fast. The naming part is the dog, because that is who the sentence is about, and the action part is ran fast, because that tells what the dog does.
If a part is missing, it is not a complete sentence. The big dog. What did it do? Ran fast. Who ran? Put the parts together: The big dog ran fast. Now it is complete!
Every sentence ends with an end mark. A period ends a telling sentence. A question mark ends an asking sentence. And an exclamation point shows a strong feeling, like wow!

science.text: Matter comes in three states: solid, liquid, and gas. A solid keeps its own shape. A liquid flows and takes the shape of whatever cup you pour it into. A gas spreads out to fill all the space it can.
Water is amazing because it can be all three states. When it is frozen, ice is a solid. When you pour it, water is a liquid. And when it boils away, steam is a gas.

Water moves in a cycle. The sun warms the lake, and water rises as vapor. That’s evaporation. Up high, the vapor cools into tiny drops that make clouds. That’s condensation. When the drops get heavy, they fall as rain. That’s precipitation!

Plants make their own food! Leaves catch sunlight, roots soak up water, and leaves take in a gas called carbon dioxide. Using the sun’s energy, the plant turns them into sugar, and gives off the oxygen we breathe. That’s photosynthesis!

kCounting.text: Let's count the apples. Touch each apple one time. One. Two. Three. Four.
The last number tells how many. We stopped at four. So there are four apples!
Your turn! Here come some fish. Count them with your finger.
This is the number three. Three is one, two, three. Let's find three!

kShapes.text: This is a triangle. It has three straight sides. And three pointy corners!
This is a square. It has four sides, all the same size. And four corners!
This is a circle. It goes round and round. No sides, and no corners!
Some shapes are flat, like a square on paper. Some shapes are solid, like a box. This solid shape is a cube!

kLetters.text: Letters have names! Here is the letter A. Here is B. And here is C.
Letters come big and little. This is big B. This is little b. They are both B!
Listen to how these words start. Ball. Bear. Bus. They all start with B!
Your turn! Listen to the start of each word. Does it start like ball?

kRhymes.text: Listen to the end of each word. Cat. Hat. Bat. They sound the same at the end. They rhyme!
Moon and spoon rhyme, too. Moon, spoon! Now you find a rhyme.
Words have parts. Let's clap them! Ti… ger. Tiger has two claps!
Your turn! Clap the parts of banana. Ba… na… na!

kTracing.text: Let's trace! Find the green dot. That is where we start.
Follow the arrow. Big line down. Then a little line across. That's L!
Now O. Start at the green dot. Go around like a C. Keep going, all the way around. That's O!
Your turn! Start at the dot, and follow the arrow. You can do it!

kAddTake.text: Three frogs sit on a log. Two more hop on! Now there are five frogs.
Five ducks swim in the pond. Then two swim away. Bye, ducks!
This is a ten frame. It has ten spots. Seven are full. Three more make ten!
Your turn! Six spots are full. Look at the empty spots.

kStoryMath.text: Listen to a story. Bear has two apples. Fox brings her three more!
Let's act it out. Put them together and count. One, two, three, four, five. Five apples!
Owl sees six birds in a tree. Then two birds fly away.
Your turn! Bunny has three pears and two peaches.

kCompare.text: Is there a cookie for every friend? Let's line them up. One, two, three.
One friend has no cookie. More friends, fewer cookies. Now one more cookie. They are the same!
Your turn! Here come bears and balls. Does every bear get a ball?
Numbers can be more, too. Four dots, seven dots. Seven is more!

kTeens.text: This is a ten-frame. It has ten boxes. When every box is full, that's a full ten!
A full ten, and three more. Ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen. Ten and three more is thirteen!
Your turn! Look at the full ten. Then count on.
Every teen number is ten and some more. Let's find twelve!

kMeasure.text: Look at the two snakes. Let's line them up at the start. Now look at the ends. This snake is longer!
Your turn! A snake and a caterpillar. They start at the same place.
Now two towers. One stands on a box. Stand them on the same ground. This tower is taller!
This is a scale. The heavy side goes down. The light side goes up!

kSorting.text: Sorting means putting things that go together. Animals go in this box. Food goes in that box!
Now count each group. Let's count the animals!
We can sort by color, too. Red ones go here. Blue ones go there!
Look at the two groups. Count each one. Which group has more?

kScience.text: Look at the sky! It can be sunny, rainy, snowy or windy.
Uh oh, rain! We want to stay dry. Your turn!
Plants need sun and water. Animals need food, water and a home.
A push moves it away. A pull brings it close. Your turn!

kTowers.text: Critters are coming down the path! Let's keep them away from the house.
Tap a spot. Answer the question. Pop! A tower!
Your turn! Count the critters with your finger.
Towers stop the critters. Tap a tower to make it stronger!

g1Adding.text: Eight plus three. Start at eight. Count on: nine, ten, eleven!
Your turn! Two plus nine. Turn it around: start at nine.
Eight plus five. Move two to make ten. Ten and three is thirteen!
Your turn! Six and six. That is a double.

g1Subtract.text: Nine take away three. Cross out three. Six are left!
Your turn! Twelve minus three. Hop back three.
Thirteen minus five. Think addition! Five plus eight makes thirteen. So the answer is eight.
Your turn! Three, five and eight are a family.

g1StoryMath.text: Bear has eight apples. Fox brings five more. Eight plus five is thirteen!
Your turn! Owl saw twelve birds. Some flew away. Now nine are left.
Bunny picks four tulips, six roses and three daisies. Four and six make ten. Ten and three is thirteen!
Your turn! Bear has nine pears. Fox has six pears.
